title: Functions

youtube.title: C++ Functions: Write Code Once, Use It Many Times | C++ Programming EP 21
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a function, call a function many times and declare a function before main, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Functions · 1:25 Your first function · 2:37 The call and the return · 3:15 Second program · 4:34 Recap · 5:04 Bug of the Day · 6:01 Challenge · 6:24 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we stop repeating ourselves. A function is a named block of code that you can call whenever you want.

scenes.onScreen: "Functions": numbered lines (1. A function is a named block of code; 2. You call it by its name; 3. It runs, then control returns) and an analogy card: a tea stall menu: one recipe, many cups
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A function is a named block of code. You write it once, and you call it by name as often as you like. When the function ends, the program returns to the line after the call. A function that gives nothing back has the type void. Think of a tea stall. There is one recipe, and it makes many cups. Why do programmers write functions? A long program becomes hard to read. Functions cut it into small parts, and each part has a name. When you need the same job again, you call the name, and you do not copy the code. Every program you have written has one function already. It is main. Now you learn to write your own.
points: A function is a named block of code
You call it by its name

scenes.onScreen: greet.cpp: a void function prints a greeting
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] The word void means this function gives nothing back. Greet is the name. The empty brackets mean it takes nothing in. [HL 5] The body prints a line. [HL 9] In main, we call greet by its name. The program jumps to the function. [HL 10] We call it a second time. The line prints twice, and we wrote it once. [HL 4] Read the first line as a label. It says the type that comes back, the name, and the inputs. [HL 5] Everything between the braces is the body, and it runs only when someone calls the function. [HL 9] A call is the name with round brackets. Do not forget the brackets, or the compiler reads the name as a plain word. If you change the message in the body, both calls change together.

scenes.onScreen: a flow: main calls greet, greet runs, control returns
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: Follow the path. Main reaches the call. The program jumps into greet. Greet prints its line. Then control returns to main, to the line after the call. Notice the jump. The program leaves main, runs the body, and comes back to the exact place where it left. It is like a bookmark. The computer remembers where to return, so you do not have to.

scenes.onScreen: order.cpp: a declaration lets main come first
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] This line is a declaration. It tells the compiler that tea exists, and it ends with a semicolon. [HL 7] Now main can call tea, even though the body comes later. [HL 11] The full definition sits below main. Without the declaration, the compiler would not know the name tea at line seven. [HL 4] A declaration is only a promise. It names the function, the inputs and the type, but it has no body. Large programs keep declarations at the top, or in a header file. [HL 11] The body can sit anywhere below, in the same file or in another file.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as order dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints One cup of tea. Notice that the declaration prints nothing. Only the call in main makes the output.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A function is a named block of code. Two. You call it by writing its name and brackets. Three. Void means the function gives nothing back. Four. Declare a function before you call it. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A function is a named block of code.
You call it by writing its name and brackets.
Void means the function gives nothing back.
Declare a function before you call it.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Calling a function before it exists
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Main calls tea, but the function is written below main. The compiler says tea was not declared in this scope. It reads from top to bottom. Add a declaration above main, or move the whole function above main. The compiler reads the file once, from the top. It has no memory of the lines below. So any name must appear before it is used. You have two easy fixes. Move the function up, or write a short declaration above main.

scenes.onScreen: I wrote a function to make tea. It returns void, and my cup is empty.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I wrote a function to make tea. It returns void, and my cup is empty.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: write a function that prints a banner
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function called banner. It prints a line of stars. Call it before and after a message. Hint: write the function above main, so you need no declaration. Write your answer in the comments.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

order.cpp: In function 'int main()':
order.cpp:5:5: error: 'tea' was not declared in this scope
    5 |     tea();
      |     ^~~
bug.why: The compiler reads the file from top to bottom. It must see a function name before the line that uses it.
